short.ours: Whip, bridle, rod: three lines built alike
short.main: Whip and bridle for beasts, the rod for fools

ours.words: and a rod for the backs of fools!

main.words: A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey,
and a rod for the backs of fools!

about.ours: The three lines are built alike: a tool, then the one it is for. The first two are beasts that need correcting and holding in. The third sets fools beside them, so the rod fits a fool as the whip and bridle fit the horse and the donkey.
about.main: The two lines are built alike: a tool, then the one it is for. The first names two beasts that need correcting and holding in. The second sets fools beside them, so the rod fits a fool as the whip and bridle fit the horse and the donkey.

evidence.ours: Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): a change in Nineveh and in God's dealings is shown, in condescension to men, as a change in God, who does not change. Calvin: God is said to repent as men can grasp it, Scripture fitting our understanding. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes): no real change in God, whose threats are conditional. Bullinger files God's relenting in Jeremiah 18:8 under Anthropopatheia.

evidence.ours: Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the LORD's repentance shows no changeableness in God but the sorrow of the divine love at sin, as 15:29 makes plain. Henry says it is a change not of God's mind but of His method, the change being in Saul. Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says God treats men as if He repented. Spence (Ellicott) says verse 11 speaks in human language.

ours.means: the murder itself, known to God, calling for His justice though Abel is silent and no one accuses Cain

ours.at: Prosopopoeia: human actions given to inanimate things, p. 864
ours.quote: “The voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.” See under Heterosis. So in verse 11. The earth is represented as opening her mouth to receive the blood of Abel.
ours.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

ours.quote: He speaks as if the blood itself were both witness and prosecutor, because God's own knowledge testified against him and God's own justice demanded satisfaction. … Though they hold their peace, their blood has a loud and constant cry, to which the ear of the righteous God is always open.

yet even when he who is injured is silent the injuries themselves are alone sufficient to arouse God to inflict punishment. … Abel was speechless when his throat was being cut, or in whatever other manner he was losing his life; but after death the voice of his blood was more vehement than any eloquence of the orator.

evidence.ours: Bullinger lists the verse under Epizeuxis as the first of ten names said twice in Scripture, seven of them by God to men, Jacob, Moses and Samuel among them: the figure calls special attention to the person and to a solemn moment of importance.
evidence.main: Bullinger lists the verse under Epizeuxis: when thus used, the figure calls special attention to the person and to a solemn moment of importance.

about.ours: God promises to redeem Israel “with an outstretched arm.” Since a man's strength lies so largely in his arms, the arm spoken of God stands for His mighty power, stretched out in His judgments to strike Egypt and set Israel free.
about.main: God promises to redeem Israel “with an outstretched arm.” Since much of a man's strength is in his arms, the arm spoken of God stands for His mighty power, stretched out in His judgments to strike Egypt and set Israel free.

ours.quote: four questions chiastically arranged. The absolute being of God … may be either inferred per ratiocinationem, or learned per traditionem. … knowledge which it might acquire even in a natural way … the teaching of revelation and tradition … The first two questions are construed with futures, the other two with perfects; the former refer to what is possible, the latter to what is an actual fact.
